question: A 52-year-old patient with BMI 34 kg/m² and type 2 diabetes has completed 6 months of supervised lifestyle modification with only 3% weight loss. Which is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy for both obesity and glycaemic control?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Orlistat is a reasonable first-line obesity pharmacotherapy but inhibits fat absorption and has predominantly GI side effects. It does not address glycaemia directly. In a patient with type 2 diabetes, a GLP-1 receptor agonist is preferred for dual benefit.

answers.text: Add a GLP-1 receptor agonist (e.g., liraglutide or semaglutide)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. GLP-1 receptor agonists (liraglutide 3 mg for obesity; semaglutide 2.4 mg subcutaneous for obesity) reduce weight by 10–15% or more AND improve glycaemic control — making them the preferred choice when obesity co-exists with type 2 diabetes. Pharmacotherapy is indicated after ≥3–6 months lifestyle modification with <5% weight loss.

Bariatric surgery is indicated at BMI ≥37.5 kg/m² (Asian-Indian) without comorbidities, or ≥32.5 kg/m² with at least one obesity-related comorbidity. This patient's BMI is 34, which meets surgical criteria only if comorbidities are present — pharmacotherapy is the appropriate next step before surgical referral.

Topiramate-phentermine (Qsymia) is not approved in India. Current Indian pharmacotherapy options include orlistat, GLP-1 receptor agonists (liraglutide, semaglutide), and — pending approval — naltrexone-bupropion. GLP-1 RAs are preferred when diabetes coexists.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review obesity pharmacotherapy: after ≥3–6 months lifestyle modification with <5% weight loss, pharmacotherapy is indicated. GLP-1 receptor agonists (liraglutide/semaglutide) are preferred when type 2 diabetes co-exists, offering dual metabolic benefit.

Well done. GLP-1 receptor agonists are preferred obesity pharmacotherapy when type 2 diabetes co-exists — they deliver both weight loss (10–15%+) and glycaemic benefit. The 5% threshold is the minimum clinically meaningful weight loss.
